newsitem.title: UK: IBCA rates Nat Power, PowerGen A plus.
newsitem.headline: IBCA rates Nat Power, PowerGen A plus.

text.p: IBCA, the European rating agency, said on Tuesday it had assigned long-term A plus and short-term A1 ratings to PowerGen Plc and National Power Plc.
(Following is the full press release from IBCA.)

London: IBCA, the European rating agency, has assigned short-term and long-term ratings to National Power plc and PowerGen plc, as follows: National Power plc: long-term A+, short-term A1; PowerGen plc: long-term A+, short-term A1.

National Power (NP) and PowerGen (PG) were created as part of the privatisation of the UK electricity industry in 1989, which separated generation, transmission and local distribution. The privatisation process also allowed competitive bidding for wholesale electricity, encouraging new entrants. As the two conventional fuel-generators in England & Wales, NP and PG received more than 70% of the UK's then extant generating capacity, primarily consisting of coal-fired plant. This share has since dipped to below 50%, following:
- the voluntary mothballing and closure of old coal-fired
plant by NP and PG;
- the expansion of nuclear capacity; and
- the arrival of cheaper, more efficient gas-fired capacity, built by independent generators.

In addition, in an attempt to promote further competition, both generators were encouraged by the UK electricity regulator to dispose of six Gigawatts (GW) of capacity during FY96 (c.16% of their then combined capacity) to an independent generator.

NP and PG still retain substantial strength in the crucial "mid-merit" segment, that part of the wholesale market which generally determines the overall pool price, and carries higher margins, while new entrants have been relegated to lower margin baseload operation.
However, the undertaking to lease out 6GW, all of which was leased to distributor Eastern Group plc, in effect created a third "Genco".
Pool prices are now regularly set by four generators, with the inclusion of Mission Energy's Pumped Storage generators, in contrast to the previous dominance of NP and PG.
Dramatic increases in productivity at both groups' power stations have also seen real profitability grow sharply, with operating margins more than doubling between FY91 and FY96.

Despite sizeable capex programmes, notably for environmental upgrades to coal plant (GBP1.7bn for NP, GBP1.3bn for PG), prodigious cash generation, helped by destocking of coal supplies in the past few years, allowed both companies to build up substantial cash resources.

Both thwarted in their attempts to expand vertically in acquiring a distribution company, attention switched to overseas investments, where both have acquired interests in between 6GW-7GW of gross generating capacity.

NP has favoured the US and Pakistan, while PG has made substantial investments in Germany and Indonesia. Both have also invested heavily in projects in the Portuguese and Australian markets. These investments are generally funded on an equity/debt split of 20:80.

NP's controlling interests in a number of projects saw GBP662 in non-recourse debt, and GBP270m in minority interest consolidated onto the H197 balance sheet, in contrast to PG, where the size of stakes has kept all overseas project investments off balance-sheet.

Following the blocked takeover bids for UK distributors, both companies also embarked on balance sheet restructuring exercises, which have seen share repurchases totalling GBP699m for NP, and GBP668m for PG.

NP declared a 1 special dividend, totalling GBP1.2bn and payable in H197, while PG have announced plans for a further 10% share buyback (costing c.GBP400m) for H297. The ratings reflect strong underlying cash generation and stability in the UK generating business for both groups, with regulatory risk receding following the latest regulator-inspired disposal.

NP and PG do not, however, enjoy the same monopoly constituency as their utility peers enjoy in their electricity distribution and water and sewerage sectors, and consequently, the implications of increasing competitive forces within the generating industry have also been incorporated into the ratings published today.

With regard to the "windfall tax" - threatened by the UK opposition Labour party, were it to take office after the next General Election, to be held by May 1997 - IBCA independently examined the impact of a tax take, solely for water and electricity companies, of GBP5bn in its recently published Electricity Sector report.

On the basis of these figures, IBCA does not believe that a windfall tax at this level, in line with market expectations, would substantially impact either NP or PG's underlying creditworthiness, and we would not, therefore, anticipate an automatic rating action following the imposition of a tax at these levels.
